headline: Rips grinding, drum gone quiet, but Delaware Bay weakfish are the real story
subhead: The ocean side is a slog right now — the back bay is where I'd spend my week.
body_markdown:
Grade for the Rips this week: C-minus. Fishable, not fun. If you want the honest read before you burn gas and bait money, that's it right there. The bass have gone deep and nocturnal on us, which is exactly what late July does — surface water's pushing into the mid-70s off the Point and out past the Rips, and stripers don't want any part of that. We're marking fish on the meter down around the thermocline break, 40 to 55 feet depending where you sit on the tide, but getting them to eat during daylight has been a fight. I had one charter Tuesday morning working the outgoing at the Rips, bucktails and Ava jigs bounced right on bottom, and we scratched out two schoolies and lost what felt like a better fish that just came unbuttoned in the current. That's the story right now — a bite, not a blitz.

If you want a shot at something better than a schoolie, you're fishing the front of the incoming tide at first light or working into dark, live-lining bunker or eels off the drop at the Rips and along the Cape May Point bar. That's when the bigger fish will come up off the structure to feed before the sun gets high and pushes them back down. Don't waste your good bait on the middle of a bright afternoon tide — I don't care how many boats are stacked up out there, most of them are marking fish they can't buy a bite from.

Bluefish have been the more dependable ocean-side player. We flagged this pattern building and it's still running — bunker schools are getting pushed tight to the beach and the blues are all over them, working from the barrier islands right up into the Wildwood surf and out past Hereford Inlet. If you're fluke fishing the Inlet and marking bait balls getting hammered on the surface, switch over — a wire leader and a Hopkins spoon or a bucktail with a rind will get bit fast. That bite should hold as long as the bunker stay pinned against the beach, and with this warm, stable stretch of weather I don't see them scattering yet.

Speaking of fluke — Hereford Inlet and the reef sites off Cape May have been steady, not spectacular. You've got to sort through a pile of shorts to find keepers, and the better fish are sitting deeper on the channel edges and humps where the water stays a touch cooler. Five-inch Gulp in white or pink shad on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the last two hours of the ebb, has been the ticket. The bite windows are tight around the tide change — you get maybe 45 minutes of good current speed before it either dies or rips too hard to hold bottom cleanly.

Now for the real news, and it's not on the ocean side. Delaware Bay's weakfish are doing something I haven't seen in a few years — and we called this two weeks ago when the bay water first pushed into the mid-70s. It's holding, and it's building into a legitimate pattern, not a one-day pop. Back-bay channels around Fortescue and up toward the mouth of the Maurice River are holding weakfish mixed in with croaker and summer flounder right on the drop-offs and channel edges. Best action is coming on the tide change — that dead slack window when the water stacks up and bait gets funneled along the edge. Bloodworms or FishBites on a simple high-low rig, fished right on bottom in 12 to 18 feet, is putting weakies in the boat. Some of these fish are pushing 4 pounds, which for Delaware Bay these days is a real fish.

The black drum run, on the other hand, has gone quiet on us. That's the honest truth — May and early June were the show for drum this year, and by late July the bulk of that spawning push has cleared out of the traditional spots off Brandywine Shoal and the deeper holes toward the mouth of the bay. If you're still targeting drum specifically, you're fishing for stragglers, and I wouldn't plan a whole trip around it right now. Save that program for next spring.

Looking at the week ahead — if this warm, settled weather pattern holds like it's been holding, I expect the weakfish bite in the bay channels to keep climbing. That's where I'd put my time if I only had one day. On the ocean side, I'd fish the Rips at first light on the incoming, live bait if you can get it, and treat anything after 9 a.m. as bonus fishing rather than the main event. And keep an eye on those bunker schools along the beach — wherever they're sitting tight, the blues won't be far behind, and that's about as sure a thing as we've got right now.
